title: How an Officer's Decision Divided the State of Wyoming
description:

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

The footage was released several months after the Wyoming Division of Criminal Investigation reported potential police misconduct. This video will compile those findings with the edited footage released by the Thermopolis Police Department. The release details Sergeant Mike Mascorro's career, a 24-year Air Force veteran with eight years in the Thermopolis Police Department, including two as a sergeant, making him second in command. It also provides essential context, describing an investigation into methamphetamine use and distribution at the town's McDonald's. Reports further detail Sergeant Mascoro suspected this after arresting McDonald's employee Derek Collins, pursuant to a warrant. During the arrest, a glass pipe was found, and Derek allegedly claimed it belonged to another employee at the restaurant. Reports do not indicate if specific names were provided. Buck's mother and wife soon gained community support. An online petition by citizen Jason Bowman, calling for Mascorro's removal, drew over 3,800 signatures, nearly one and a half times Thermopolis's population. A small protest followed and at a town council meeting on the issue, residents were split between praising Mascooro and calling for his resignation. One notable comment made by Mike Chimenti, a former mayor of the town and self-proclaimed policeman for 43 years, stated he, never saw as many write-ups or arrest for drugs, or seen the drug trafficking and druggers scared of this community like they have been since he went to work. Wyoming has extremely strict restrictions on the release of body camera footage, but finally, 10 months after the incident, the body camera footage presented in this video was released. Mascoro reportedly performed administrative duties at that time. Four months later, and 14 months after the incident, a town press release announced his full-duty reinstatement. It'd be another 10 months or two years after the incident that Buck's mother Deborah Laramore Fenton and his wife Brandy Laramore filed a civil lawsuit to sue Mascorro and the Thermopolis Police Department for wrongful death. The suit claims Mascoro, and to an extent the department violated Buck's rights with a warrantless search, used excessive force, caused negligence and emotional distress. They are asking for $3 million in damages. This seemingly led the town council to vote on Mascaro's resignation. After a reportedly heated floor debate, only one member voted against resigning him. Eight days after the civil lawsuit was reported by local news, Mascoro resigned. Roughly a month later, post-commissioners held a separate vote on Mascooro retaining his peace officer certification. The commission unanimously voted to decertify Mascooro, preventing him from being an officer in the state of Wyoming. The post commission can be quoted saying it should be noted too. Mascooro denies any wrongdoing. It's a simple certification surrender. The civil case is still open and is being handled by the fifth judicial district court for Hot Springs County. And people might say that the sergeant made a decision that should have never gone that far, but from where I stand, this didn't need to be a fatal encounter. And a different decision might have brought about a peaceful conclusion, but instead two people collided and unfortunately the badge became the spark that lit the fuse. A single decision bust through the door or hold the line. Every cop's had that moment and every veteran knows it's the moment that defines you. If Mr. Laramore refused, identify himself Sergeant Moscaro could have cited him for interference and went about his day. Now, was Mr. Laramore innocent in all this? Absolutely not. However, this could have went down very differently. And people love to say that cops have to make tough calls, and they do, but not every tough call needs to end with a trigger pull. Sometimes restraint is the hardest move you'll ever make because calm authority and adrenaline always fight to take over. That's the real battle no training can prepare you for, the one between discipline and dominance. Thermopolis is in a city where stories disappear. It's a place where everyone knows the echo. People talk, they question and they stop trusting and in that doubt the bond between police and public starts to crumble. Now seeing a cop go down is always hard to watch. Nobody wants to see that. It cuts deep every single time because behind the vest is a human being who put their life on the line. But when the investigation is over, we are forced to ask some sub questions and we might not like the answers. And that's the part that separates the motion from truth. but too many people run from that reality but we have to face it because that's what true accountability looks like
